_doc: Port policy for the upstream radar (scripts/upstream-radar.ts). Fix and performance changes always enter semantic triage. Feature additions enter only when their touched files avoid every diverged surface whose blocksCleanFeatures flag is not false. This screen creates a review candidate, not a merge decision. titleAllowRegexes and cleanFeatureTitleAllowRegexes classify unprefixed upstream titles.

divergedSurfaces.name: model catalog, IDs, types, and roles
divergedSurfaces.note: veyyon owns its model catalog, IDs, tiers, roles, and provider discovery. Port underlying correctness fixes onto local structures; never import upstream tables or generated model files.

divergedSurfaces.name: credential storage and OAuth routing
divergedSurfaces.note: veyyon uses SQLite multi-credential storage with selection, backoff, and session affinity. Preserve those contracts when adapting a fix.

divergedSurfaces.name: session, model-control, and instrumentation lifecycle
divergedSurfaces.note: veyyon owns session persistence, resumability, model controls, and fail-closed instrumentation. Adapt fixes without weakening those invariants.

divergedSurfaces.name: tool, capability, extension, and discovery architecture
divergedSurfaces.note: veyyon uses ToolSession, the built-in registry, capability discovery, native Bun loading, and local manifest compatibility. Port behavior through those owners instead of importing upstream factories.

divergedSurfaces.name: interactive TUI composition
divergedSurfaces.note: veyyon's status line, controller split, and interactive versus ACP/RPC behavior diverge. Leaf TUI fixes may still adapt, but upstream feature composition is not an automatic candidate.

divergedSurfaces.name: native crates and worker infrastructure
divergedSurfaces.note: veyyon's renamed crates, native surface, and worker-host contract require explicit semantic mapping.

divergedSurfaces.name: branding, install, website, and CI
divergedSurfaces.note: veyyon's brand, distribution, website, and workflows are locally owned. Never import upstream naming, release channels, or CI direction.

divergedSurfaces.name: documentation
divergedSurfaces.note: Rewrite documentation for veyyon's behavior and terminology instead of copying upstream prose.

neverPorted._doc: Paths a port PR may not author. veybot's port and ci_repair prompts carry these constraints; the post-hoc `land` audit that used to verify them was retired with the Jules manager, so a stray path is now caught by the human who reviews the candidate rather than by a program. A port of one upstream bug fix touches the source that holds the bug, its test, and its changelog entry, so anything listed here came from the agent's environment rather than from the fix. What a stray path proves depends on its tier. `quarantine` paths are always noise: an agent running an older bun rewrites `configVersion` in bun.lock, and agents leave scratch helpers at the repo root (#201 shipped 14 beside a good one-file fix); the fix still lands once they are dropped. `owned` paths belong to main and a port has no business rewriting them, but a single hit is usually harmless drift such as the `Verified against <sha>` freshness stamp #196 refreshed in docs/internal/releasing.md, so one or two are treated the same way. `refuseThreshold` or more of them at once means something else entirely: the branch is a whole-tree revert, which is what a stale clone produces when it resolves `merge main` in its own favour. #184/#186/#187 hit 183, 248 and 183 owned paths, and #195/#199/#200 hit 66 each. Such a diff must be refused outright rather than filtered, because the same staleness that reverted the docs also reverted source files that no path list can recognise: #184 quietly reverted packages/argot and packages/catalog too. Note that crates/vendor/ is deliberately absent. veyyon carries uu-rm as vendored source, so a real fix can and does live there (#185).
